codex.worst_flaw: The reward can encourage rushed checks, but the audit relies on existing records and cannot detect hazards technicians miss or omit.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design gives only three weeks of staggered comparison across a few crews. It sets no sample-size or uncertainty plan, does not address spillover between crews, predefines no cost or harm thresholds, and has no independent shadow validation or versioned event history to support the counts.

holistic.reason: The proposal fixes workflow barriers first, gets union and steward input, protects against gaming with spot-checks and clear counting rules, and uses a staggered rollout with a decision metric after rewards end, but a one-hour crew reward is modest and awareness relies mostly on toolbox talks and the app.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is unsafe to launch because the audit relies on the same records that determine payout and can miss rushed all-clear checks or job starts recorded after work actually began.

claude.worst_flaw: The 75% team threshold gives every crew member the same lunch, with feedback shown at weekly huddles. That creates peer pressure on individual technicians, and the design never checks for small-crew inference or effects on morale, while the audit and appeal process depends on one coordinator and keeps no replayable event history.

holistic.reason: Unusually well-designed for a unionised workforce, with union co-design, friction fixes before rewards, safety-stop credit, gaming audits and a pre-set decision rule, but the lunch is a weak, small incentive and the process is operationally heavy, so awareness and durability beyond the workflow fixes are uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design compares reward and delayed-reward teams for only two weeks, with no sample-size, clustering or uncertainty plan, and 10 sampled checks a week across about 300 technicians is too thin an audit to reliably catch rushed checks; there are also no replayable event or policy versions behind the corrections.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout can proceed on digital adoption alone without requiring evidence that checklist quality and safe stop-work behavior hold up after rewards end.

holistic.reason: Union-involved, safety-first design with fallbacks, privacy, audits and a randomized rollout is very approvable, but the one-paid-hour reward is modest and the heavy process adds complexity, while durability depends on fixing app usability rather than the incentive.

claude.worst_flaw: A whole-team, all-or-nothing half-day reward hangs on an 85% threshold with no pre-registered uncertainty or sample-size reasoning. The squad stagger is confounded by the shared pooled prize, so the reward's added value over the queue fixes alone is never cleanly isolated.

codex.worst_flaw: Announcing a shared reward to all squads before their staggered start dates can change review behaviour in the comparison squads, making the reward’s added effect hard to estimate.

holistic.reason: The workflow fixes (routing, protected review blocks, a rotating reviewer) and the staggered rollout are credible and engineer-friendly, but the rules are long, the spot-checks and exception handling add overhead, and a half-day off for a team target may seem arbitrary to sceptics, with only a moderate chance the behaviour holds once the prize ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot reliably isolate the lunch reward’s effect because the single-queue comparison is vulnerable to changes over time and the two-queue comparison leaves baseline differences and case mix unaddressed.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design rests on a non-randomised two-queue stagger (or a directional before/after comparison) over two weeks, with no sample-size, uncertainty or cost and harm outcomes defined in advance. That leaves the incremental value of the lunch reward over plain queue fixes largely unidentified.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, private feedback, a team-wide lunch and a quality guard suit sceptical engineers and should plausibly lift the on-time rate, but the rules are intricate, the reward is modest and the hand-sampled audit is a burden, so the habit may fade once the lunch and the primary/backup rota stop being actively managed.

claude.worst_flaw: The audit design has gaps: there is no replayable event history or policy versioning, appeals go to the same rotation owner who also does the sampling, and five samples per group with a two-of-five pause threshold give a weak signal for detecting gaming.

codex.worst_flaw: The core metric blocks launch because starting the clock at the review request lets delayed or missing requests hide time that review-ready PRs spend waiting.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with co-designed quality standards, team-level reward, no leaderboard, randomized stepped rollout, and routing/protected-time fixes that persist after prizes end, though it is detailed enough that the audit and sampling burden and a small reward (one hour off) could make it feel fiddly to sceptical engineers.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot tell whether nurses reliably log eligible hand-hygiene moments because kiosk counts lack a matched opportunity denominator and observer audits measure hand-hygiene compliance.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward is tied to observer-audited compliance from a small, Hawthorne-prone monthly sample. The design names no staffed appeal route and no versioned audit-correction history, and it never checks whether kiosk logs are valid or worth collecting. As a result, the kiosk system the hospital asked for is never validated, and payout disputes have no transparent resolution path.

holistic.reason: Well-governed design with verified audit-based payouts, safeguards against gaming and care delays, privacy protections, and a staggered rollout that can show whether gains persist, but the shared meal reward is modest and the behaviour is likely to fade without ongoing reinforcement.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk retention decision relies on unvalidated matching by ward, time and moment type, which can credit unrelated entries and miss valid logs delayed by patient care.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward depends on just two monthly audits per ward per period, which gives a small, noisy observation sample, and the design never sets a minimum observed-opportunity count or a variance rule for the reward decision (it sets one only for the kiosk adoption sample), so wards can win or lose on chance.

holistic.reason: Fair ward-level reward with a staggered design, privacy protections and sensible safety pauses is approvable, but a small meal and thank-you plus a heavy measurement apparatus may not drive strong engagement or last once rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: Ward-level audit compliance with only two small monthly observer samples gives weak case-mix handling and no auditable event/policy versioning or staffed appeal path, so reward decisions may rest on noisy, Hawthorne-affected observations.

codex.worst_flaw: The meal is awarded on observed compliance, so a ward can earn it by improving only while observers are present, and the design has no check for that possibility.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with audited outcomes, shared team rewards, independence safeguards and a stop rule, but the modest meal reward is easy to overlook, the audit-only pay-off is distant from kiosk use, and gains may fade once the prize ends despite the workflow fixes staying in place.

codex.worst_flaw: Customer-data exposure is a launch blocker because detection relies on a small post-publication sample and the only immediate action specified is to pause reward credit.

claude.worst_flaw: A team-wide paid-time-off reward for a 35% link rate creates peer pressure to inflate links, and the only check against that is a 10-ticket weekly QA sample across all teams, which is too small to catch irrelevant links reliably or to back the pause rule.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design (QA sampling, CSAT checks, workflow fixes first, randomized rollout, keeps workflow after rewards end) but a one-hour team reward is modest, the 35% target triples the 12% baseline, and the heavy measurement and rules overhead may dull motivation.

codex.worst_flaw: The uniform 40% threshold makes paid time off depend on ticket mix and small-sample luck because the design adjusts for ticket volume alone.

claude.worst_flaw: The 90-minute paid time off is all or nothing at 40%, yet only 12 credited tickets are checked each week across 60 agents, so agents are pushed to attach loosely relevant links and the check will rarely catch it; agents with few or zero eligible tickets are also left unhandled.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with quality sampling, staggered rollout, private feedback and workflow fixes, but 90 minutes of time off for a 4-week window is a modest, somewhat delayed reward and the 40% target is a big jump from 12%, so awareness and durable habit after rewards end are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: Sampling eight credited tickets per week across all teams can leave a team eligible for payout even if its only audited article link fails the quality check.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says how leave, outages, uneven case mix, or agents and teams with few eligible tickets are handled, so the 50% team threshold and per-agent progress can be unfair or all-or-nothing. Its eight-ticket weekly audit across 60 agents is also too thin to catch gaming reliably before payout.

holistic.reason: It fixes the workflow first, ties credit to approved articles with sampled quality checks, keeps CSAT and reviews out of the reward, and uses a staggered start with set decision bands, but a team-level paid hour off is a modest incentive and the four-week window may not be enough for agents to keep linking articles once the reward ends.
